question: A 55-year-old woman comes to the emergency room 30 minutes after the sudden onset of chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. Prior to the onset of her symptoms, she was lying in bed because of a migraine headache. Episodes of similar chest pain usually resolved after a couple of minutes. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. Her only medication is sumatriptan. An ECG shows ST-segment elevations in the anterior leads. Serum troponins are negative on two successive blood draws and ECG shows no abnormalities 30 minutes later. Administration of which of the following is most likely to prevent further episodes of chest pain in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Migraine headache -> vasospasm -> chest pain radiating to left shoulder -> 70% CHAIN: Smoking -> increased risk of cardiovascular disease -> chest pain -> 80% CHAIN: ST-segment elevations in anterior leads on ECG -> myocardial infarction -> chest pain -> 90% CHAIN: Negative serum troponins -> early phase of myocardial infarction -> chest pain -> 80% CHAIN: Sumatriptan use -> vasoconstriction -> chest pain -> 70% CHAIN: Clopidogrel administration -> antiplatelet effect -> prevention of further episodes of chest pain -> 70%
enhanced_information: The patient's chest pain is likely due to myocardial infarction, supported by ST-segment elevations on ECG and negative serum troponins. Sumatriptan use may contribute to vasoconstriction. Clopidogrel administration, with its antiplatelet effect, is most likely to prevent further episodes of chest pain in this scenario.
analysis: The patient presents with chest pain, ST-segment elevations on ECG, and negative troponins, suggestive of unstable angina or non-ST elevation myocardial infarction. Given the likely vasoconstrictive effect of sumatriptan and the need for antiplatelet therapy, clopidogrel is the most appropriate choice to prevent further episodes of chest pain in this scenario.
